factor_ratings.evidence: Manages a 4-person RTL sub-team on the NX-400 digital front-end; impact confined to the sub-team and its block-level deliverables, not the broader function.
Runs sprint planning and code review sign-off for the group -- operational team management, no evidence of setting direction beyond the sub-team's defined workstream.
Problems are scoped to a single RTL sub-team's deliverables (clock/reset architecture, sprint execution) -- defined workstream, not cross-team or strategic ambiguity.
Personally owns clock/reset architecture RTL for the block -- deep in one discipline (digital design), no described breadth across disciplines.
Owns a block (clock/reset architecture RTL) end to end across a development cycle, consistent with subsystem/block-level ownership rather than a full subsystem or product.
Influence is within the immediate team -- code review sign-off and performance reviews for direct reports; no described influence on adjacent teams or partners.
4 direct reports, all individual contributors, no budget authority beyond headcount requisitions -- matches M3 anchor of 4-10 ICs, no budget authority.

decision.governing_rule: rule 5: manager level is not automatic from headcount -- span corroborates but scope of impact and problem complexity (both M3-level here) govern the assignment
decision.alternative_reasoning: M4 was considered given the manager title and the fact the person still personally owns significant RTL (could suggest a hybrid tech-lead/manager scope), but M4 requires 10-25 people or a program budget and broader scope across teams -- neither is present here. The 4-person, single-sub-team, no-budget profile clearly caps at M3 under rule 2 (lower level governs a split) since scope of impact is not unambiguously at the higher level.
decision.reasoning: All seven factors converge cleanly on M3: a 4-person all-IC sub-team, no budget authority beyond requisitions, sprint-level operational management, and personal ownership of a single block (clock/reset architecture RTL) rather than a subsystem or product. This matches the M3 anchor (4-10 direct reports, all ICs, no budget authority) and the L4 IC-equivalent scope (owns a subsystem/complex workstream) is not exceeded -- the person owns a block, which is sub-L4/M3 territory on factor 5a but the managerial scope of impact (leading a defined sub-team on a single block) still nets to M3 rather than a lower non-manager-track outcome, since people management begins at M3 and the span/scope evidence doesn't stretch to M4 (which requires 10-25 people or a program budget). Title 'Engineering Manager' is treated as evidence only, not as the level itself (rule 6); the described scope -- a small sub-team, block-level ownership, no budget -- is what drives the M3 assignment. Source org context (104 employees, late-stage private, whole company) fits the 'small company, under ~150' archetype where titles often map down 1-2 levels; here the described scope independently supports M3, which is consistent with (not contradicted by) that prior, so confidence is not reduced on that basis.
